notes.meaning: Just before this, Micah warned that the temple hill would become a wild, empty place (3:12). Now comes hope. "The last days" points to the time of the Messiah, God's promised King, when Christ came and built His church. The mountain is "raised" in honor, not in height, because God rules and teaches from it. People will keep flowing to it like a river, a steady stream of believers from everywhere.

Nations that once ignored Israel's God now urge each other, "Come, let us go." They don't just send others; they go together. They come to be taught God's ways and promise to walk in them. The "law" and "word" going out from Jerusalem is the good news about Jesus. It began there, where He preached, died, rose again, and poured out His Spirit, and then spread to the whole world. A true church is one where people are taught by God's pure word.

God, through Christ, settles disputes between nations. His word shows them where they are wrong. Fierce people become gentle, and weapons are turned into farm tools. Calvin notes they don't just stop hurting others; they start doing good. This has begun wherever the gospel takes root. But wars have not yet ended. The sources say full peace waits for Christ's return and heaven.

Sitting under your own vine and fig tree is a picture of peace, safety, and plenty. People will be so safe they won't even need a roof; they can rest out in the open fields. The words echo the peace of Solomon's reign and God's promise in Leviticus 26:6. It may sound too good to be true, but the LORD Himself has said it, so it will happen.

Other nations hold tightly to their own false gods. God's people decide to hold even more tightly to the true God, forever. Even if the whole world goes another way, believers should stay firm. Our faith rests on God's word, not on what most people think. To walk "in the name of the LORD" also means living in His strength.

God pictures His people as hurt, limping sheep, scattered far away. He admits He is the one who struck them for their sins. And because He wounded them, He can also heal and gather them. The "remnant" (a small group that survives) will grow into a strong nation. The LORD Himself will reign over them forever. This was fulfilled in Christ, who is both David's son and God. Matthew Henry sees it in the believing Jews and the far-off Gentiles gathered into one church.

differ.view: These promises point not only to the church but also to a future day when the Jewish people as a nation turn to Christ.

notes.meaning: The "watchtower of the flock" stands for Jerusalem, where God's flock gathered. It is like a shepherd's tower, where he watches over his sheep. Some link it to a tower near Bethlehem (Genesis 35:21). The "former dominion" means a kingdom as great as David's and Solomon's. This came true in Christ, who was given David's throne. His kingdom is spiritual, ruling through His word over the whole world.

Micah looks ahead to a time of terror, when enemies come against Jerusalem. Zion cries out like a woman in labor because her king is gone or can do nothing to help. Losing the king hurt deeply, because God's promises were tied to David's throne. Wesley adds a comfort: even with no earthly king, God, their true King, is still with them.

The pain is real. The people will leave the city, camp in open fields, and be carried off to Babylon. But labor pains lead to birth, not death. Micah repeats "there": the very place of their suffering will be where God rescues them. God did this through King Cyrus. To "redeem" means to buy back and set free, and this rescue points ahead to our greater freedom through Christ. Micah named Babylon while Assyria was still the great power, which the sources see as a mark of true prophecy.

Many nations gang up against Zion. They want to see her shamed and ruined, so they can gloat over her. This happened after the return from exile, when neighbors tried to stop the rebuilding, and again in later times. Calvin says God's people should not lose heart when enemies boast as if God has left them.

The enemies don't know God's plan. They think they are gathering to destroy Zion. But God is gathering them like bundles of grain onto a threshing floor, the place where grain is beaten. People often mean one thing while God means the opposite. So believers should not judge what God is doing by the boasting of the wicked.

Back then, grain was threshed by oxen trampling it. Zion is pictured as an ox with iron horns and bronze hooves. When God gives His people a job, He gives them the strength to do it. The riches taken from the enemies are given to God, not kept for selfish gain. Matthew Henry sees this in the gospel's victory over the powers of darkness. Calvin and the Geneva Notes say it will be fully fulfilled at Christ's return.
